title: Not Ashamed of the Gospel
subtitle: Romans 1:1–17
description: Paul's longest greeting introduces him to a church he has never visited, and the thesis of the whole letter lands in two sentences.
paragraphs: Paul writes this letter from Corinth, in the three months he spends in Greece at the end of his third journey. The collection for Jerusalem is gathered, and he is about to carry it up himself. Beyond Jerusalem his road runs west: Rome, which he has tried to reach for years and never has, and beyond Rome, Spain. This letter goes ahead of him to a church he did not plant and has never seen. Its last chapter commends the woman who carries it, Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port. A scribe will sign his own name near the end. First, the longest greeting Paul ever writes, because this church knows him only by report, and the greeting has to introduce him.

It begins with his name and his three titles. “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, and set apart for the gospel of God,” the gospel “He promised beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures.” The promise was always about a person: “regarding His Son, who was a descendant of David according to the flesh, and who through the Spirit of holiness was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord.” Through him came the commission that defines Paul's work: “we received grace and apostleship to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith.”

The readers stand inside that call already: “And you also are among those who are called to belong to Jesus Christ.” The greeting proper names them twice over with the same word: “To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Loved by God, called to be saints. The letter will spend sixteen chapters unfolding what those two phrases carry.

Then the thanksgiving, and it is about reputation. “First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed all over the world.” A church in the capital, and its faith is news everywhere. Paul's prayers for them are constant, and his witness is God himself: “God, whom I serve with my spirit in preaching the gospel of His Son, is my witness how constantly I remember you in my prayers at all times, asking that now at last by God’s will I may succeed in coming to you.”

The visit he wants is not one-directional. “For I long to see you so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you, that is, that you and I may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith.” The delay is explained once and plainly: “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, how often I planned to come to you (but have been prevented from visiting until now), in order that I might have a harvest among you, just as I have had among the other Gentiles.” Underneath the longing sits an obligation that explains the whole journey west: “I am obligated both to Greeks and non-Greeks, both to the wise and the foolish. That is why I am so eager to preach the gospel also to you who are in Rome.”

Then the letter's thesis, the two sentences everything else in Romans unpacks. “I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek.” And inside the gospel, its revelation: “For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish, just as it is written.” The written words are Habakkuk's, and Paul sets them over the whole letter like a title: “The righteous will live by faith.”

title: The Downward Exchange
subtitle: Romans 1:18–32
description: The wrath of God revealed against a world that suppressed the truth and exchanged glory downward, answered three times by a handing over.
paragraphs: The thesis of the first episode had two halves, and the letter takes the darker one first. “The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness.” Suppress is the charge: the truth is not missing, it is being held down. “For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse.”

The fall Paul describes is an exchange, made step by step. “For although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him, but they became futile in their thinking and darkened in their foolish hearts. Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles.” Worship did not disappear. It moved downward, from the immortal God to pictures of things that die, and finally to things that crawl.

God's response to the exchange is stated three times, and it is a handing over. “Therefore God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity for the dishonoring of their bodies with one another.” The reason is the exchange itself: “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is forever worthy of praise! Amen.” The second handing over follows the same grammar: “For this reason God gave them over to dishonorable passions.” Paul names the shape of it in the sexual life of the culture: women exchanging natural relations for unnatural ones, men abandoning natural relations and burning with lust for one another, “Men committed indecent acts with other men and received in themselves the due penalty for their error.”

The third handing over is the widest. “Furthermore, since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, He gave them up to a depraved mind, to do what ought not to be done.” Then the catalogue, and it runs far past the sexual sins into the whole fabric of ordinary life: “They have become filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed, and depravity. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice. They are gossips, slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, and boastful. They invent new forms of evil; they disobey their parents. They are senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless.”

The last verse is the floor of the descent. The knowledge was never lost, and the conduct is not ignorant: “Although they know God’s righteous decree that those who do such things are worthy of death, they not only continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them.” The exchange that began with glory ends with applause: a culture no longer merely doing the things, but honoring them. It is the portrait of the world the gospel of the first episode has arrived to save, and Paul has aimed it, so far, at the Gentile world his readers would most readily nod along with. The next episode turns it around.

title: No Excuse
subtitle: Romans 2:1–16
description: The argument turns on the reader who judged too quickly: God's kindness misread, a judgment by deeds, and a law written on Gentile hearts.
paragraphs: The trap closes on the reader who agreed too quickly. “You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another. For on whatever grounds you judge the other, you are condemning yourself, because you who pass judgment do the same things.” The catalogue of the last episode turns out to have been a mirror held up for a second audience: everyone who judges. God's judgment, Paul says, is not like ours: “we know that God’s judgment against those who do such things is based on truth.”

Then the question that exposes the judge's hope: “So when you, O man, pass judgment on others, yet do the same things, do you think you will escape God’s judgment?” Behind the escape plan sits a misreading of God's patience: “Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” Kindness treated as indulgence becomes its opposite: “because of your hard and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed.”

The standard of that day is quoted from the Psalms and stated as a settled rule: God “will repay each one according to his deeds.” Both outcomes are laid out in the same first-for-the-Jew, then-for-the-Greek order the gospel itself was announced in. “To those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality, He will give eternal life. But for those who are self-seeking and who reject the truth and follow wickedness, there will be wrath and anger. There will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek; but glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek. For God does not show favoritism.” Privilege changes the order of hearing. It does not change the standard.

The law divides the world for judgment, but not into safe and unsafe. “All who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law, and all who sin under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous.” Then the observation that unsettles both sides: “Indeed, when Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. So they show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them on the day when God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel.”

The episode ends where it aimed: secrets. The day Paul describes does not weigh public records but hidden ones, judged through Christ Jesus, and conscience, accusing or defending, is presented as a preview of that courtroom, not a replacement for it. The judge of chapter 2's opening has no excuse, the hearer of the law has no shelter, and the Gentile with no law has a witness inside him. Next, Paul turns to the person holding the strongest claim of all: the one who bears the name itself.

title: The Heart Is the Matter
subtitle: Romans 2:17–29
description: The bearer of the name is cross-examined, circumcision is weighed, and true Jewishness is relocated from the flesh to the heart.
paragraphs: Now the argument names its hearer. “Now you, if you call yourself a Jew; if you rely on the law and boast in God; if you know His will and approve of what is superior because you are instructed by the law; if you are convinced that you are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, because you have in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth.” The sentence builds the whole identity before it asks its first question, and the questions come like cross-examination: “you, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?”

Isaiah supplies the verdict on the pattern: “God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.” The name of God, carried by a people whose conduct contradicts it, becomes material for mockery among the very nations the instruction was meant to light.

Then circumcision, the sign itself, is weighed. “Circumcision has value if you observe the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.” The sign's value is real and conditional at once. And the reversal follows: “If a man who is not circumcised keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision? The one who is physically uncircumcised yet keeps the law will condemn you who, even though you have the written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker.” The outsider who does the thing will stand in judgment over the insider who only bears the sign of it.

The chapter ends by relocating the whole identity. “A man is not a Jew because he is one outwardly, nor is circumcision only outward and physical. No, a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code. Such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God.” Outward and inward, flesh and heart, written code and Spirit: the pairs run through the end of the chapter and set up everything Paul will argue about the law's true purpose.

Between the last episode and this one, the argument has now covered the judge, the hearer, the Gentile conscience, and the bearer of the name. Every shelter has been examined from inside. The obvious objection comes next, and Paul stages it himself: if all of this is true, what advantage is left in being a Jew at all, and can God be trusted to keep his word to a people like this?

title: Every Mouth Silenced
subtitle: Romans 3:1–20
description: Objections staged and answered, a chain of Scripture hung verse by verse, and the law's verdict silences every mouth.
paragraphs: Paul stages the objection himself, the way he will throughout this letter. “What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision?” The answer surprises in its warmth: “Much in every way. First of all, they have been entrusted with the very words of God.” Entrusted: the oracles were a trust, and the question that follows is whether Israel's failure cancels the Trustee's faithfulness. “What if some did not have faith? Will their lack of faith nullify God’s faithfulness? Certainly not! Let God be true and every man a liar. As it is written.” Then David's words, quoted standing alone: “So that You may be proved right when You speak and victorious when You judge.”

The objectors press it into absurdity, and Paul lets them. If human unrighteousness highlights God's righteousness, is God unjust to judge? “I am speaking in human terms,” he notes, mid-argument. “Certainly not! In that case, how could God judge the world?” If my lie makes God's truth shine brighter, why am I still condemned? The slander version of his own gospel gets the sharpest sentence in the chapter: some claim that we say, “Let us do evil that good may result.” “Their condemnation is deserved!”

Then the summation of the whole case so far. “What then? Are we any better? Not at all. For we have already made the charge that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin.” What follows is not Paul's vocabulary but Scripture's, a chain of quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah hung one after another until the whole human frame is covered. “There is no one righteous, not even one. There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God. All have turned away, they have together become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.”

The chain moves down the body. Speech first: “Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit.” “The venom of vipers is on their lips.” “Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.” Then movement: “Their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery lie in their wake, and the way of peace they have not known.” Last, the eyes: “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” Throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, eyes, and behind them all a mind that does not understand and a will that does not seek.

The conclusion is courtroom language. “Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God.” The law's speech was never a ladder offered to its hearers. Its purpose in this argument is a verdict: “Therefore no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law. For the law merely brings awareness of sin.” Every mouth silenced is not the end of the letter, though. It is the silence into which the next two words are spoken: but now.

title: Justified by Faith
subtitle: Romans 3:21–31
description: But now: a righteousness revealed apart from the law, an atoning sacrifice that proves God just, and boasting structurally excluded.
paragraphs: “But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, as attested by the Law and the Prophets.” The turn of the whole letter is two words long, and Paul is careful about what kind of new thing it is: new in its revealing, old in its witnesses. The Law and the Prophets themselves testify to it. “And this righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no distinction, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”

Justified freely, by grace, through redemption: three layers of gift-language in one sentence. The center of it is a presentation. “God presented Him as an atoning sacrifice in His blood through faith, in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand.” The cross answers a question about God, not only about sinners: for generations he had passed over sins, and the passing over could look like indifference until this demonstration. “He did this to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.” Just, and the justifier. The judge's character and the defendant's pardon are vindicated in the same act.

The consequences are argued as quickly as they are drawn. “Where, then, is boasting? It is excluded. On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith. For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law.” Boasting is not scolded out of existence; it is structurally excluded, because the ground of the verdict is faith, not works, and faith leaves nothing to display.

The door this opens is measured by monotheism itself. “Is God the God of Jews only? Is He not the God of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too, since there is only one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith.” One God, therefore one way of justification for both peoples, the distinction of the last three chapters dissolved at exactly the point where it mattered most.

The last objection of the chapter is the law's own honor: “Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law.” Faith does not tear the law down; it establishes what the law was for. How that works, Paul proves from the law's own first story, and it begins with a name the next episode takes up: Abraham, the forefather, and what he discovered.

title: Abraham Believed God
subtitle: Romans 4:1–25
description: The forefather's ledger: faith credited as righteousness before circumcision, so that one man fathers two families by one faith.
paragraphs: The proof comes from the family album. “What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has discovered?” If the forefather was justified by works, he had a boast, “but not before God.” Scripture's own sentence is quoted as the whole case: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”

Paul unpacks the accounting word, credited, with a wage. “Now the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation. However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.” Wages are owed. Abraham's entry was made on the other ledger: not to a worker, but to a believer, by the God who justifies the ungodly.

David is called as the second witness, describing the same blessedness from its other side: “Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him.” Righteousness credited apart from works, and sin not counted: the two descriptions meet.

Then the timing question, and the whole genealogy turns on it. “Is this blessing only on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised? We have been saying that Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness. In what context was it credited? Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before.” Circumcision arrived after the crediting, as its sign and seal: “he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised.” So Abraham fathers two families by one faith: “he is the father of all who believe but are not circumcised,” and “also the father of the circumcised who not only are circumcised, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.”

The promise's route follows the same line. “For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not given through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith.” The law came centuries after the promise, and it cannot retroactively become the promise's condition. “Therefore, the promise comes by faith, so that it may rest on grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring,” of the law and of the faith together. “He is the father of us all. As it is written.” Then the promise's own words, quoted alone: “I have made you a father of many nations.”

The chapter's second half looks at the believing itself. The God Abraham trusted is described before the trust is: “the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist. Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed and so became the father of many nations, just as he had been told.” The second promise quoted: “So shall your offspring be.” Paul is honest about the evidence against the hope: Abraham “acknowledged the decrepitness of his body (since he was about a hundred years old) and the lifelessness of Sarah’s womb. Yet he did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God, being fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised. This is why ‘it was credited to him as righteousness.’”

And the record, Paul insists, was kept for later readers. “Now the words ‘it was credited to him’ were written not only for Abraham, but also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited,” for us, that is, “who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.” The forefather's ledger entry becomes the pattern of the family's faith, and the object of that faith now has a name and an empty tomb.

title: Peace With God
subtitle: Romans 5:1–11
description: The verdict spent: peace, access, a standing in grace, suffering that ends in hope, and a love proved while we were still sinners.
paragraphs: “Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand. And we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God.” Peace, access, a standing place in grace, and a hope aimed at glory: the chapter opens by spending the verdict of the last three episodes, and the spending starts with rejoicing.

The rejoicing runs in an unexpected direction next. “Not only that, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope. And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us.” The chain from suffering to hope is not left as bare logic. Its last link rests on something poured in: God's love, in the heart, through the Spirit already given.

The proof of that love is timed. “For at just the right time, while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man someone might possibly dare to die. But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” Human loyalty, at its extreme, dies for the good. This death was for the powerless and the ungodly, before any improvement, at just the right time.

From that past act, Paul argues forward, twice, with the same measure. “Therefore, since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him! For if, when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!” Enemies reconciled by his death will not be abandoned by his life. The harder thing is done; the greater thing follows from it.

The passage closes where it opened, on rejoicing, but the object has grown. “Not only that, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.” The first episode of this letter promised a righteousness revealed. Here its recipients are found standing in grace, patient inside suffering, and rejoicing in God himself. Next the argument steps back to the widest frame it has: not Abraham now, but Adam, and the one man through whom death entered, weighed against the one Man through whom the gift came.

title: In Adam, In Christ
subtitle: Romans 5:12–21
description: Two men, two reigns: the trespass that reached everyone weighed against the gift that abounds to the many, deliberately uneven.
paragraphs: “Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.” The sentence starts a comparison it does not finish; Paul breaks off to establish the ground first. “For sin was in the world before the law was given; but sin is not taken into account when there is no law. Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the way that Adam transgressed. He is a pattern of the One to come.” Death's reign across the lawless centuries is the evidence: something entered with the one man that reached everyone after him. Adam is named a pattern, a first instance of a shape, of the One who was still to come.

Then the comparison resumes, and its first word is a refusal. “But the gift is not like the trespass. For if the many died by the trespass of the one man, how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many!” The two sides of the scale are deliberately uneven. Trespass and gift work in opposite directions and at different weights.

Paul runs the imbalance twice more. “Again, the gift is not like the result of the one man’s sin: The judgment that followed one sin brought condemnation, but the gift that followed many trespasses brought justification.” One sin behind the judgment; many trespasses behind the gift. “For if, by the trespass of the one man, death reigned through that one man, how much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ!” Death reigned. The receivers of the gift will reign in life. The reign itself changes hands.

Only then does the interrupted sentence of verse 12 get its completion, in a balanced pair of summary lines. “So then, just as one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men. For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous.” One man's disobedience, one Man's obedience, and the many carried in each direction.

The law's place in the long story is fixed in two sentences at the end. “The law came in so that the trespass would increase; but where sin increased, grace increased all the more, so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” The law entered alongside, not at the foundation, and its effect was to multiply the trespass it measured. Grace answered at a higher rate. Two reigns stand over the human story now, death's and grace's, and the question the next chapter opens with takes the second reign's generosity as its problem: if grace abounds where sin increases, why not sin on?

title: Dead to Sin
subtitle: Romans 6:1–14
description: Grace is not a license: a death already happened in baptism, and the deposed king's orders are to be refused by people alive to God.
paragraphs: The objector returns with the obvious misuse of the last episode's math. “What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not! How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?” Paul's answer is not a rule but an event: a death has already happened, and the place it happened was baptism. “Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.”

United runs in both directions. “For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection. We know that our old self was crucified with Him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, that we should no longer be slaves to sin. For anyone who has died has been freed from sin.” The logic is stark: the dead are beyond a master's reach. Slavery ends at death, and the old self's death was a crucifixion, shared with Christ.

Christ's own death and life set the pattern's terms. “Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with Him. For we know that since Christ was raised from the dead, He cannot die again; death no longer has dominion over Him. The death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God.” Once for all, and never again: that is what makes the pattern habitable.

Then the argument turns into an instruction about identity: “So you too must count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.” Count yourselves: the verb is an accounting term, and the reckoning is the bridge between the event and the conduct. The conduct follows immediately: “Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey its desires. Do not present the parts of your body to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life; and present the parts of your body to Him as instruments of righteousness.” Sin is treated as a deposed king still issuing orders to a mortal body. The refusal is active: the same members once presented to it are now presented, as instruments, to God.

The ground of the whole charge is stated as a change of jurisdiction: “For sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace.” And that last phrase gives the objector his next opening. If not under law but under grace, why not sin freely? Paul takes the question up in the next episode, and his answer is the most uncomfortable word in the chapter: slaves.

title: Slaves of Righteousness
subtitle: Romans 6:15–23
description: No one is masterless: set free from sin and enslaved to God, with the chapter's famous account of wages and gift.
paragraphs: “What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not!” The answer this time is a definition of freedom nobody in the room expected. “Do you not know that when you offer yourselves as obedient slaves, you are slaves to the one you obey, whether you are slaves to sin leading to death, or to obedience leading to righteousness?” Obedience is never masterless. Every life is serving one of two outcomes, and the master is identified by the direction.

For these readers, the transfer has already happened. “But thanks be to God that, though you once were slaves to sin, you wholeheartedly obeyed the form of teaching to which you were committed. You have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness.” Set free from sin, slaves to righteousness: the freedom and the slavery are the same event described from its two sides.

Paul apologizes for the picture even as he uses it. “I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh.” Then he works it practically: “Just as you used to offer the parts of your body in slavery to impurity and to escalating wickedness, so now offer them in slavery to righteousness leading to holiness.” The body parts remember their old employment. The new service uses the same members, the same presenting, for the opposite fruit.

The old freedom gets its true name on review. “For when you were slaves to sin, you were free of obligation to righteousness. What fruit did you reap at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? The outcome of those things is death.” Free of obligation to righteousness: the independence the old life boasted in is reclassified as the slavery itself, and its harvest is shame and death.

Against it, the new service and its harvest: “But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves to God, the fruit you reap leads to holiness, and the outcome is eternal life.” Then the chapter's last line, the most quoted sentence in Romans, drawn as two columns of an account. Wages on one side, a gift on the other: “For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Sin pays what is earned, on time and in full. God gives what is not. The chapter that began by forbidding grace as an excuse ends by sharpening grace into a contrast no wage can imitate, and the argument returns to the law itself: what it could do, what it could not, and the strange war it set going inside a man.

title: The Law and the Struggle
subtitle: Romans 7:1–25
description: The law acquitted and sin indicted, then the war in the first person: the good wanted and not done, and a cry for rescue.
paragraphs: The law binds only the living; Paul starts there, with marriage as the working picture. A wife is bound to her husband while he lives; “if her husband dies, she is free from that law and is not an adulteress if she marries another man.” Death dissolves the jurisdiction. The application carries the same shape: “Therefore, my brothers, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, that you might belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit to God.” Under the old arrangement, the passions the law aroused bore fruit for death. “But now, having died to what bound us, we have been released from the law, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code.”

The objector is ready: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Indeed, I would not have been mindful of sin if not for the law. For I would not have been aware of coveting if the law had not said.” The commandment quoted is the tenth, standing alone: “Do not covet.” But naming the sin woke it. “But sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire. For apart from the law, sin is dead. Once I was alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died. So I discovered that the very commandment that was meant to bring life actually brought death. For sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through the commandment put me to death.”

The law is acquitted in terms, and sin is indicted in its place. “So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good. Did that which is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not! But in order that sin might be exposed as sin, it produced death in me through what was good, so that through the commandment sin might become utterly sinful.” The law's work in the story is exposure: it made sin visible as sin, at full strength, using a good instrument.

Then the war, told in the first person and left in it. “We know that the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin. I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do.” The doing and the wanting have come apart, and the analysis is unsparing. Doing what he does not want carries its own verdict about the law, and about the real actor: “In that case, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it. I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh; for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out. For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do.”

Paul names the discovered principle like a law of physics: “When I want to do good, evil is right there with me. For in my inner being I delight in God’s law. But I see another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind and holding me captive to the law of sin that dwells within me.” The chapter that began with the law's jurisdiction ends inside a captivity, and the cry that escapes is not for instruction but for rescue: “What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!” Then the honest summary, left standing exactly as he gives it: “So then, with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.” The next chapter opens with the verdict the whole struggle was waiting for, and its first word is Therefore.

title: Led by the Spirit
subtitle: Romans 8:1–17
description: No condemnation: the law of the Spirit of life, minds set two ways, adoption, and a child's cry in Jesus' own language.
paragraphs: “Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit of life set you free from the law of sin and death.” The war of the last episode is answered by a verdict and a transfer: a new law, in the sense of a new governing power, has freed the captives from the old one. What the first law could not do, God did: “For what the law was powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin. He thus condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.” Sin was condemned in the flesh of the Son so that the law's righteous standard could be fulfilled in people who walk by the Spirit.

The chapter sorts humanity by its set of mind. “Those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace, because the mind of the flesh is hostile to God: It does not submit to God’s law, nor can it do so. Those controlled by the flesh cannot please God.”

Then the address turns personal, and conditional. “You, however, are controlled not by the flesh, but by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ. But if Christ is in you, your body is dead because of sin, yet your spirit is alive because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead is living in you, He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit, who lives in you.” The Spirit is named three ways in three verses, of God, of Christ, of Him who raised Jesus, and his presence in a mortal body is presented as the down payment on that body's resurrection.

The obligation runs one direction only. “Therefore, brothers, we have an obligation, but it is not to the flesh, to live according to it. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.”

Sons, and the word carries the chapter home. “For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship, by whom we cry.” The cry itself is quoted, in the language Jesus used for his Father: “Abba! Father!” “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children. And if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,” and here the sentence turns on a condition the letter does not remove, “if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.” Slavery behind, adoption ahead, an inheritance waiting, and suffering named as the road's present condition. The next episode takes that suffering up and sets it against the glory, with all of creation groaning in the same key.

title: Nothing Can Separate Us
subtitle: Romans 8:18–39
description: Creation groaning, believers groaning, the Spirit groaning, and a courtroom reversed: the list of things that cannot separate.
paragraphs: “I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us. The creation waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God.” The scale is cosmic from the first verse. Creation itself was dragged into the frustration: “For the creation was subjected to futility, not by its own will, but because of the One who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God.”

The groaning is universal, and Paul distributes it carefully. “We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time. Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.” Childbirth is the chosen picture: pain with a delivery inside it. “For in this hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what he can already see? But if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it patiently.”

The third groaning belongs to the Spirit himself. “In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.”

Out of the groaning rises the chapter's most carried sentence: “And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.” Its chain follows, five links with no gaps: “For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers. And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.” The purpose behind the working is conformity to the Son, and the last link is spoken in the past tense, as if the glory were already settled.

Then the courtroom of chapter 3 reopens, with the verdict reversed. “What then shall we say in response to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things? Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is there to condemn us? For Christ Jesus, who died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God,” and here Paul's own sentence adds, “and He is interceding for us.”

The closing list of would-be separators is exhaustive on purpose, and the psalm quoted inside it is the church's oldest song of suffering: “For Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.” The answer covers every item and category: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Eight chapters of argument land there: nothing in all creation. The next three chapters turn to the question that could undo it all in the readers' minds: if God's word is this sure, what happened to Israel, to whom the promises were made first?

title: Sorrow and Unceasing Anguish
subtitle: Romans 9:1–33
description: Paul's grief for Israel opens the letter's hardest argument: election, mercy, hardening, and a potter who answers the clay.
paragraphs: Before the argument about Israel, Paul stops to swear to his grief. “I speak the truth in Christ; I am not lying, as confirmed by my conscience in the Holy Spirit. I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood, the people of Israel.” The inventory of their privileges follows, and it is the fullest in Scripture: “Theirs is the adoption as sons; theirs the divine glory and the covenants; theirs the giving of the law, the temple worship, and the promises. Theirs are the patriarchs, and from them proceeds the human descent of Christ, who is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.” The apostle to the Gentiles begins his hardest chapter by cataloguing what Israel was given, and wishing himself accursed in their place.

The question is stated as a defense of God's word. “It is not as though God’s word has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel. Nor because they are Abraham’s descendants are they all his children. On the contrary.” Then Genesis, quoted standing alone: “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” “So it is not the children of the flesh who are God’s children, but it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring. For this is what the promise stated.” And the promise's words: “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.”

The second family story is pressed harder. Rebecca's twins were chosen between before either had a record: “Yet before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, in order that God’s plan of election might stand, not by works but by Him who calls, she was told.” The oracle to Rebecca: “The older will serve the younger.” And Malachi's later word on the two nations: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

The objector's protest is the one every reader makes, and Paul stages it: “What then shall we say? Is God unjust? Certainly not! For He says to Moses.” The Exodus answer is quoted whole: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” “So then, it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy.” Pharaoh is the counter-case, in Scripture's own words to him: “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” “Therefore God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden.”

The objection sharpens: “Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?” The reply is not an explanation but a boundary: “But who are you, O man, to talk back to God? Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it.” The clay's question, quoted: “Why did You make me like this?” “Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use?” What follows is given as a pair of open questions, and the telling leaves them in Paul's interrogative form: what if God bore with great patience the vessels of wrath to make his glory known to the vessels of mercy, “whom He prepared in advance for glory,” a company the next verse names: “including us, whom He has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles?”

Hosea then speaks for the called Gentiles, in the prophet's own astonishing reversal: “I will call them ‘My People’ who are not My people, and I will call her ‘My Beloved’ who is not My beloved,” “and, ‘It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’’” For Israel, Isaiah's word is a remnant word: “Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved. For the Lord will carry out His sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively.” And the older Isaiah line: “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.”

The chapter's conclusion is the paradox the next two chapters exist to explain. “What then will we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith; but Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness, has not attained it. Why not? Because their pursuit was not by faith, but as if it were by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written.” Isaiah's stone, quoted last: “See, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.”

title: The Word Is Near You
subtitle: Romans 10:1–21
description: Zeal without knowledge, a righteousness that forbids the climb, a confession in heart and mouth, and hands held out all day long.
paragraphs: “Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation. For I testify about them that they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge. Because they were ignorant of God’s righteousness and sought to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes.” Zeal is not the lack. Paul testifies to the zeal himself. The tragedy he names is a zeal aimed at establishing a righteousness of their own, passing by the one God offers.

Moses is called to state the law's own terms, in Leviticus' words: “The man who does these things will live by them.” Then the righteousness that is by faith is given a voice of her own, and she quotes Deuteronomy back with her meaning supplied in parentheses. She forbids the two imaginary journeys: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down) or, ‘Who will descend into the Abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).” No climbing, no descending; Christ is neither fetched nor retrieved. “But what does it say? ‘The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,’ that is, the word of faith we are proclaiming.”

The confession itself is stated in its two parts, heart and mouth. Paul writes that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart, “that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. For with your heart you believe and are justified, and with your mouth you confess and are saved.” Isaiah underwrites it: “Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” And the scope is the letter's refrain: “For there is no difference between Jew and Greek: The same Lord is Lord of all, and gives richly to all who call on Him, for.” Joel's promise, quoted: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

Then the chain of questions that has sent missionaries ever since, each link requiring the one before it. “How then can they call on the One in whom they have not believed? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach? And how can they preach unless they are sent? As it is written.” Isaiah's line on the messengers: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”

But the chain's success is not the chapter's ending. “But not all of them welcomed the good news. For Isaiah says.” The prophet's own question: “Lord, who has believed our message?” “Consequently, faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.” Did Israel hear? “But I ask, did they not hear? Indeed they did.” The psalm answers: “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.” Did Israel understand? Moses answers first, from the Song: “I will make you jealous by those who are not a nation; I will make you angry by a nation without understanding.” Isaiah answers boldly: “I was found by those who did not seek Me; I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me.” And for Israel herself, the picture God gives of his own posture closes the chapter, held all day long: “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people.” The hands stay out. The next chapter asks the question the whole section has been circling: has God, then, rejected his people?

title: The Olive Tree
subtitle: Romans 11:1–36
description: A remnant by grace, a fall that enriched the world, wild branches warned against boasting, and an argument that ends on its knees.
paragraphs: “I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew.” The first proof is the author. The second is Elijah, at his lowest, appealing against Israel: “Lord, they have killed Your prophets and torn down Your altars. I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well.” The divine reply corrected his arithmetic: “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” “In the same way, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace. And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.”

For the rest, the seeking failed and the hardening is described in Scripture's own stacked words: “What Israel was seeking, it failed to obtain, but the elect did. The others were hardened, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear, to this very day.’ And David says: ‘May their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution to them. May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever.’”

But the fall is not the end of their story, or of the world's. “I ask then, did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Certainly not! However, because of their trespass, salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous. But if their trespass means riches for the world, and their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much greater riches will their fullness bring!” Paul turns to the Gentile readers directly: “I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am the apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in the hope that I may provoke my own people to jealousy and save some of them. For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?”

Then the tree. “If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch; if the root is holy, so are the branches. Now if some branches have been broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others to share in the nourishment of the olive root, do not boast over those branches. If you do, remember this: You do not support the root, but the root supports you.” The imagined Gentile reply is staged and answered: “Branches were broken off so that I could be grafted in.” “That is correct: They were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but be afraid. For if God did not spare the natural branches, He will certainly not spare you either.”

The tree's logic runs toward regrafting, not away from it. “Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God: severity to those who fell, but kindness to you, if you continue in His kindness. Otherwise you also will be cut off. And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. For if you were cut from a wild olive tree, and contrary to nature were grafted into one that is cultivated, how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!”

Then the mystery, stated and, per this letter's rule, left as stated: “I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, so that you will not be conceited: A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written.” Isaiah and Jeremiah speak together in the quotation: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob. And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins.” Both/and is the chapter's verdict on Israel's present state: “Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs. For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable.” And the mercy circuit closes: “For God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone.”

What follows is not another argument but the argument's author on his knees. “O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!” Job and Isaiah supply the two unanswered questions: “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?” “Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?” And the doxology gathers everything, source, means, and end, into one sentence: “For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever! Amen.” The great Therefore of the next chapter rises straight out of that Amen: on account of all this mercy, something is now urged on the readers' bodies.

title: A Living Sacrifice
subtitle: Romans 12:1–21
description: The great Therefore: bodies offered, minds renewed, gifts measured soberly, and love's short commands reaching all the way to enemies.
paragraphs: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.” The largest Therefore of the letter stands on the doxology that closed the last episode, and the response it asks for is not a feeling but a body, presented whole, and described with a paradox: a sacrifice that stays alive. “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

The transformed mind starts with measurement. “For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but think of yourself with sober judgment, according to the measure of faith God has given you.” The measure is then illustrated by the picture Corinth also heard, a body: “Just as each of us has one body with many members, and not all members have the same function, so in Christ we who are many are one body, and each member belongs to one another.”

The gifts are listed as graces, each with its manner of use attached. “We have different gifts according to the grace given us. If one’s gift is prophecy, let him use it in proportion to his faith; if it is serving, let him serve; if it is teaching, let him teach; if it is encouraging, let him encourage; if it is giving, let him give generously; if it is leading, let him lead with diligence; if it is showing mercy, let him do it cheerfully.” Seven gifts, and the instructions are mostly adverbs: proportionally, generously, diligently, cheerfully.

Then the chapter breaks into short commands, most of them a breath long, all of them about love with its sleeves rolled up. “Love must be sincere. Detest what is evil; cling to what is good. Be devoted to one another in brotherly love. Outdo yourselves in honoring one another. Do not let your zeal subside; keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord. Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer. Share with the saints who are in need. Practice hospitality.”

The commands reach outward, to the people outside the room. “Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be proud, but associate with the lowly. Do not be conceited. Do not repay anyone evil for evil. Carefully consider what is right in the eyes of everybody. If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone.”

The last word belongs to vengeance, and it is taken out of human hands entirely. “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written.” Deuteronomy's sentence, quoted standing alone: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.” “On the contrary.” Proverbs, quoted the same way: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head.” The chapter's last line draws the whole application into a single contest: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” What the sacrifice looks like on an ordinary Tuesday, the next episode continues: taxes, debts, and the hour of the morning.

title: Put On the Lord Jesus Christ
subtitle: Romans 13:1–14
description: Authorities, taxes, and the one debt never paid off, then morning instructions for people who believe the night is nearly over.
paragraphs: The application steps outside the church's door, to the powers that govern the street. “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God. Consequently, whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, and those who do so will bring judgment on themselves.” The text is carried here as Paul wrote it, between the love commands of the last episode and the love commands that follow it in this one.

The ruler's office is described in God's terms. “For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Do you want to be unafraid of the one in authority? Then do what is right, and you will have his approval. For he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not carry the sword in vain. He is God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer. Therefore it is necessary to submit to authority, not only to avoid punishment, but also as a matter of conscience.”

Conscience, not fear, is the stated ground, and the practical bill follows from it: “This is also why you pay taxes. For the authorities are God’s servants, who devote themselves to their work. Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due.”

Then every debt is cancelled except one. “Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” The commandments Paul lists, against adultery, murder, theft, and coveting, along with any others, are gathered into Leviticus' one decree, quoted standing alone: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” “Love does no wrong to its neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.” What the law aimed at across ten thousand words, love completes in the neighbor's direction, daily, at arm's length.

The chapter's last movement changes the light. “And do this, understanding the occasion. The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber, for our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near. So let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy.”

The closing instruction is the episode's title and the application section's sharpest garment metaphor: “Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh.” Put on Christ; make no provision. Morning conduct for people who believe the day has nearly drawn. The next episode moves from the street back into the dining room, where the Roman church's own two tables, the weak and the strong, are dividing over food and days.

title: The Weak and the Strong
subtitle: Romans 14:1–23
description: Two tables in one church: contempt and judgment both forbidden, conscience honored, and freedom spent on a brother's good.
paragraphs: “Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions.” The Roman church's dividing line ran through the dinner table and the calendar. “For one person has faith to eat all things, while another, who is weak, eats only vegetables. The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him.” Two opposite temptations govern the whole passage: contempt from the strong, judgment from the weak, and both are forbidden on the same ground. God has accepted the other man.

The servant argument settles the jurisdiction. “Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.” Days come under the same rule: “One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. He who observes a special day does so to the Lord; he who eats does so to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.”

Underneath the menu fight stands the deepest fact in the chapter. “For none of us lives to himself alone, and none of us dies to himself alone. If we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. For this reason Christ died and returned to life, that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living.” Belonging to the Lord is why no believer is another believer's project or problem to grade: “Why, then, do you judge your brother? Or why do you belittle your brother? For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat. It is written.” Isaiah's oath, quoted: “As surely as I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God.” “So then, each of us will give an account of himself to God.”

The verdict Paul issues is about obstacles, not opinions. “Therefore let us stop judging one another. Instead, make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way.” And then he breaks his own neutrality for one sentence, marking it as his personal conviction: “I am convinced and fully persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. But if anyone regards something as unclean, then for him it is unclean.”

That conviction does not license the strong. It binds them. “If your brother is distressed by what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. Do not by your eating destroy your brother, for whom Christ died.” The kingdom itself is redefined away from the table: “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.” So the pursuit changes: “let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification. Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food.” The concession asked of freedom is total and specific: “It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble.”

The chapter's last word returns the disputed matters to their proper courtroom. “Keep your belief about such matters between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself by what he approves. But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because his eating is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.” Conscience is neither crushed nor crowned; it is answered to God, and the brother's conscience is treated as more important than one's own menu. The next episode opens with the strong addressed by name and given their marching orders: bear with the weak, and do not please yourselves.

title: Accept One Another
subtitle: Romans 15:1–13
description: Christ the pattern of the strong, four corners of Scripture stacked in one choir, and the God of hope prayed over a divided room.
paragraphs: “We who are strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak and not to please ourselves. Each of us should please his neighbor for his good, to build him up. For even Christ did not please Himself, but as it is written.” The psalm line Paul quotes is one Jesus' sufferings fulfilled: “The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.” The pattern of the strong is set by the strongest: self-pleasing surrendered, insults absorbed.

Scripture's role in the church's patience is stated as a principle: “For everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope.” Then the first of this section's two prayers, for the divided room: “Now may the God who gives endurance and encouragement grant you harmony with one another in Christ Jesus, so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The command that gathers the whole weak-and-strong argument follows, modeled on Christ's own act: “Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring glory to God.” Its ground runs in two directions at once. “For I tell you that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs, so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy.” Servant to the circumcised, for truth; mercy to the Gentiles, for glory. Then four witnesses from four corners of Scripture are stacked, exactly as Paul stacks them. From the Psalms: “Therefore I will praise You among the Gentiles; I will sing hymns to Your name.” From the Law: “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.” From the Psalms again: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples.” And from Isaiah: “The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.”

Jew and Gentile in one choir was written into the book from the beginning, Law, Prophets, and Writings all singing the same line. The second prayer closes the teaching of the letter the way 8:39's assurance deserves: “Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.” Everything after this is the letter's own business: why it was written, where its author is going, and a whole chapter of names.

title: To Spain by Way of Rome
subtitle: Romans 15:14–33
description: Paul's own file: a pioneer apostle's completed arc, an errand to Jerusalem, a church asked to be senders, and prayers enlisted.
paragraphs: Paul turns from teaching to his own file, and begins with a compliment he qualifies carefully. “I myself am convinced, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, brimming with knowledge, and able to instruct one another. However, I have written you a bold reminder on some points, because of the grace God has given me to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.” The boldest letter in his surviving file is framed as a reminder, written under orders.

His boasting is fenced to one subject. “Therefore I exult in Christ Jesus in my service to God. I will not presume to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me in leading the Gentiles to obedience by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, and by the power of the Spirit of God. So from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ.” Illyricum is the far northwestern edge of his arc, on the Adriatic. The strategy that governed the whole arc is named without apology: “In this way I have aspired to preach the gospel where Christ was not known, so that I would not be building on someone else’s foundation. Rather, as it is written.” Isaiah on the unannounced King: “Those who were not told about Him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”

“That is why I have often been hindered from coming to you.” The pioneer work itself was the hindrance; the map was full. “But now that there are no further opportunities for me in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to visit you, I hope to see you on my way to Spain. And after I have enjoyed your company for a while, you can equip me for my journey.” Rome is not the destination. Rome is the staging ground, and the Romans are asked to be its senders.

First, though, the unfinished errand that this whole letter was written on the eve of: “Now, however, I am on my way to Jerusalem to serve the saints there. For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem. They were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister to them with material blessings.” The collection that fills two chapters of 2 Corinthians is here a debt gladly owed, carried by the man who raised it. “So after I have completed this service and have safely delivered this bounty to them, I will set off to Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.”

He closes the section by enlisting their prayers for the road in both directions. “Now I urge you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to join me in my struggle by praying to God for me. Pray that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service in Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints there, so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and together with you be refreshed. The God of peace be with all of you. Amen.” The letter's argument is done. What remains is its warmest chapter: a page of greetings to people most of the ancient world never heard of, in a city the writer has never visited.

title: Greet Every Saint
subtitle: Romans 16:1–27
description: The letter's warmest chapter: Phoebe commended, two dozen names greeted, one sharp warning, a scribe's signature, and the doxology.
paragraphs: The letter's last chapter opens by commending its own carrier. “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea. Welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her with anything she may need from you. For she has been a great help to many people, including me.” Cenchreae is Corinth's eastern port. The longest letter Paul ever wrote most likely traveled to Rome in this woman's hands, and its first instruction is that Rome take care of her.

Then the greetings, more than two dozen names, in a city Paul has never visited. First, two he knows best. “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who have risked their lives for me. Not only I but all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them. Greet also the church that meets at their house.” The tentmakers of Corinth and Ephesus are in Rome now, with a church in their house again. “Greet my beloved Epenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia. Greet Mary, who has worked very hard for you.”

“Greet Andronicus and Junia, my fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners. They are outstanding among the apostles, and they were in Christ before I was.” Prison shared, seniority acknowledged: they were in Christ before the apostle to the Gentiles was, and he says so in writing. The roll runs on, each name carrying its own small weight of history: “Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys. Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ.” Two households are greeted by their masters' names, Aristobulus' and Narcissus', the believers in them known to Paul though the masters are not addressed. “Greet Herodion, my fellow countryman.” Then the workers: “Greet Tryphena and Tryphosa, women who have worked hard in the Lord. Greet my beloved Persis, who has worked very hard in the Lord.”

“Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.” Someone in Rome had mothered the apostle, and the letter pauses to thank her by relation. Two circles close the roll: “Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas and all the saints with them. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ send you greetings.”

Between the greetings and the end, one warning, sharp and final. “Now I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Turn away from them. For such people are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. Everyone has heard about your obedience, so I rejoice over you. But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”

The senders' side signs off last. “Timothy, my fellow worker, sends you greetings, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my fellow countrymen.” Then the scribe steps out from behind the dictation for one line of his own: “I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.” And the Corinth frame of the whole letter shows in its final greetings: “Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church, sends you greetings. Erastus, the city treasurer, sends you greetings, as does our brother Quartus.”

The letter that opened with the gospel promised beforehand closes by gathering that gospel into one doxology. “Now to Him who is able to strengthen you by my gospel and by the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery concealed for ages past but now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets by the command of the eternal God, in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith.” The obedience that comes from faith: the letter's first chapter named it as Paul's commission, and its last sentence names it as the eternal God's purpose for all nations: “to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen.”
